flashcard_questions.q: Which historical figure does Snowball represent in the allegory?
flashcard_questions.a: Leon Trotsky, commander of the Red Army.

flashcard_questions.q: Which historical conflict does the Battle of the Cowshed represent?
flashcard_questions.a: The Russian Civil War of 1918 to 1921.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Napoleon's conduct during the Battle of the Cowshed mirror Stalin's?
flashcard_questions.a: He is absent from the action, just as Stalin contributed little militarily.

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation shows Snowball's physical courage against Jones?
flashcard_questions.a: He ‘flung his fifteen stone against Jones's legs’.

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation shows Snowball winning the animals round by argument?
flashcard_questions.a: He ‘often won over the majority by his brilliant speeches’.

flashcard_questions.q: Which word means able to speak or write fluently and persuasively?
Which slogan does Snowball use to simplify debate on the farm?
Which quotation shows Napoleon working behind the scenes rather than in open debate?
flashcard_questions.a: He is ‘better at canvassing support for himself in between times’.

flashcard_questions.q: What reason does Napoleon give for taking the puppies away?
flashcard_questions.a: He says he will ‘make himself responsible for their education’.

flashcard_questions.q: Which decoration is awarded to Snowball and Boxer after the battle?
What second, darker purpose do the farm's medals and ceremonies serve?
flashcard_questions.a: They are tools of control that make it harder to question authority.

flashcard_questions.q: Which quotation shows Boxer's moral sensitivity after he strikes the stable-lad?
flashcard_questions.a: ‘I have no wish to take life, not even human life.’

flashcard_questions.q: How do the pigs later rewrite the Battle of the Cowshed?
flashcard_questions.a: Napoleon claims the credit and accuses Snowball of fighting on Jones's side.

flashcard_questions.q: Which country does the easygoing Mr Pilkington of Foxwood represent?
Which country does the tough, shrewd Mr Frederick of Pinchfield represent?

notes: 15 cards: 6 character or theme to quotation, 4 context-to-relevance (Trotsky, Stalin, Britain, Germany), 2 event-to-significance (rituals as control, the rewriting of the battle), 1 historical event card, 1 definition-front term card (eloquent), 1 cause card (the puppies). Dropped allegory, authority, rituals and tyranny as glossary cards — each is already tested through an event or quotation card, so a second direction would interfere.
